## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.73523.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.73523.sa1)

Our editorial process produces two outputs: i) public reviews designed to be posted alongside the preprint for the benefit of readers; ii) feedback on the manuscript for the authors, including requests for revisions, shown below. We also include an acceptance summary that explains what the editors found interesting or important about the work.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "IPMK physically binds to the SWI/SNF complex and modulates BRG1 occupancy" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 3 peer reviewers, including Irwin Davidson as Reviewing Editor and Reviewer #1, and the evaluation has been overseen by Jessica Tyler as the Senior Editor.

The reviewers have discussed their reviews with one another, and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this to help you prepare a revised submission.

As you can see from the comments below the referees raised several major issues that have to addressed in any revised version.

1). The referees were concerned that effects are seen only at sites with low BRG1 occupancy. To be sure that this is meaningful the referees propose in their comments below a series of further analyses of the data that should be performed.

2). SiRNA IPMK depletion is of limited efficiency with several blots showing an incomplete knockdown. This may lead to an under estimation of the possible impact IPMK has on BRG1 function. The authors should perform a full IPMK KO using CRISPR and re-assess the effects on BRG1 occupancy and gene expression. Alternatively, at the very least the authors should use a constitutive shRNA-mediated IPMK silencing to achieve a better reduction in its expression.

3). A major issue is the lack of a real functional readout on IPMK knockdown in terms of the biology of the ES cells. If as claimed genes regulated by bivalent promoters are the preferred targets this should translate into altered ES cell differentiation. The authors should investigate in detail the impact of IPMK silencing or knockout on ES cell biology to go beyond the analyses of gene expression.

Any revised version must also address the other issues raised by the referees.

Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

Several issues should be addressed.

The authors describe the effect of IPMK depletion at transcriptional start sites of bivalent and H3K4me3 only promoters. Can the authors perform the same analyses at enhancers? According to their model, enhancers show higher BRG1 occupancy, and therefore should not be affected by IPMK depletion. However, this may not be true for all enhancers, there may be a subset with lower occupancy where IPMK depletion would have a comparable effect to that seen at the TSS. The authors must also take into account that the siRNA mediated depletion is of limited efficiency, several blots showing an incomplete knockdown. Perhaps if a full IPMK KO was made using CRISPR, even sites with stronger BRG1 occupancy would now be affected. Is this possible? See below.

As IPMK depletion affects sites with lower BRG1 occupancy, it is important to exclude the possibility that IPMK depletion results in reduced expression of BRG1 or another limiting subunit leading to reduced SWI/SNF levels.

The authors show that IPMK depletion leads to a more pronounced effect on expression of genes with bivalent promoters compared to H3K4me3 only promoters. As bivalent promoters are those that are destined to be activated or repressed upon ES differentiation, this would suggest that IPMK depletion should impact ES differentiation. The authors should test this idea and ask whether IPMK depletion by siRNA or, even better shRNA to achieve stable depletion, affects ES cell differentiation. Also, the authors make no comments on how IPMK siRNA and de-regulation of around 500 genes affects ES cell physiology or proliferation. This is relevant if a CRISPR KO was to be made, are the ES cells viable or not. If yes, a KO would be a useful complement as mentioned above to assess the full effect of IPMK on SWI/SNF function and subsequent ES differentiation. These data would strongly strengthen the paper and provide a functional readout for the how IPMK affects SWI/SNF beyond gene expression assays.

Can the authors address whether the IPMK effects on SWI/SNF genome occupancy and gene expression require its enzymatic activity or whether the effects are independent of enzymatic activity?

The manuscript requires thorough re-writing and proofing by a native English speaker as the text is often difficult to follow. The study could be written in a much clearer manner.

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

1. There is only one concern about the immunoprecipitations. The BAF155 co-IP in Figure 2C is not very convincing. There is a band in the IgG control that is stronger than the band in the IP lane.

2. Details on analysis of peaks for cut and run and ATAC-seq are missing. How were the changes in peak height quantified and determined to be statistically significant.

3. The rationale and method for defining clusters and then re-clustering should be clarified.

4. RNA-seq profiles with IPMK knockdown showed that some genes occupied by BRG1 and regulated at the chromatin level are also regulated by IPMK. However, there is no information about whether the effects of IPMK depletion on gene expression results from suppression of BRG1 occupancy. Experiments to address whether BRG1 depletion affects the expression of Phactr3, Nmra1l or any of the IPMK-regulated genes determined by RNA-seq should be conducted.

5. The manuscript loses focus by conducting RNA-seq in cells with Smarcb1 depletion. These data should be integrated with the data on BRG1 occupancy and chromatin accessibility. A key question to address is whether any of the overlapping Smarcb1/IPMK regulated genes can be associated with changes in BRG1 occupancy and chromatin accessibility upon IPMK and BRG1 knockdown.

Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

To test the quality of the BRG1 CUT&RUN experiments, the authors could use the lists of typical enhancers and super-enhancers published in Whyte et al., 2013 (http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2013.03.035) and generate heat maps of BRG1 distribution showing separately each replicate of BRG1 CUT&RUN, as well as the non-specific IgG CUT&RUN control. For the comparison, they could use the previously validated GSM1581286 BRG1 ChIP-seq data.

To verify that their interpretation of low amplitude changes in ChIP-seq or CUT&RUN signal is correct, the authors should generate heat-maps as in Figure 4C and 4G showing individual replicates of both BRG1 CUT&RUN and ATAC-seq.

Similarly, the authors should also produce heat-maps of the five clusters of promoters shown in figure 5D, showing each BRG1 CUT&RUN replicate experiment, as well as non-specific IgG CUT&RUN control.

These figures will be determinant to test the validity of the differences in BRG1 enrichment observed in IPMK-depleted cells.

The description of the results of the ATAC-seq experiments at promoter elements is difficult to follow: multiple analysis are presented using different series of clusters of TSS. The authors should try to simplify this part of manuscript.

[Editors’ note: further revisions were suggested prior to acceptance, as described below.]

Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Inositol polyphosphate multikinase physically binds to the SWI/SNF complex and modulates BRG1 occupancy in mouse embryonic stem cells" for further consideration by eLife. Your revised article has been evaluated by Jessica Tyler (Senior Editor) and a Reviewing Editor.

The manuscript has been improved but there are some remaining issues that need to be addressed, as outlined below:

In this revised version, the authors have performed a number of important experiments to address previous concerns. These new data have strengthened the study and the conclusions. Specifically, they have used stable shRNA-mediated IPMK knockdown in addition to the siRNA and observed analogous effects on BRG1 occupancy. They have performed rescue experiments that show that the enzymatic activity of IPMK is not required for BRG1 occupancy and they have differentiated the shIPMK cells as embryoid bodies and provide evidence for downregulated expression of several endodermal markers. They have incorporated in their analyses BRG1 occupancy at previous lists of mESC enhancers. This new data addressed many of the major issues raised in the previous version.

Nevertheless, the authors should perform some additional revisions as several sections of the manuscript are rather difficult to follow.

1). As previously suggested, the authors should remove the data on siSMARCB1 in Figure 6 and Figure 6-supplement. This data interrupts the flow of the paper and dilutes the message. There are no analyses of how siSMARCB1 affects BRG1 or IPMK occupancy or chromatin accessibility by ATAC-seq and therefore these results cannot be properly interpreted. Also, there is no relevance in this paper for 3T3 cells. Removing this data does not affect the major conclusions of the paper and will make the paper easier to read.

2). The description of the data in Figure 5 and the Figure 5 supplements is extremely difficult to follow. All of this section needs careful attention and should be rewritten. For example, it is difficult to understand why total BRG1 loss at cluster 1 has a differential effect at bivalent and K4me3-only promoters. Why does it not impact the accessibility of the K4me3-only promoters. Figures 5F and G are particularly difficult to understand. Can this data be represented in another manner, or at least the description in the text should be improved?

3). The new experiments show reduced expression of endodermal markers in embryoid bodies generated from the shIPMK cells. The authors should comment on whether the genes that are not properly induced in the embryoid bodies displayed bivalent promoters in the ESCs and if yes, did they belong to a specific cluster as defined in Figure 5. In other words is there a relationship between altered BRG1 occupancy at the promoters in ESCs and failure to be properly induced in embryoid bodies.

4). In the discussion, the authors should avoid unnecessary speculation about how IPMK may affect SWI/SNF structure (lines 510-550). The discussion should be simplified and shortened to specifically address the results of this study (see lines 574-605).

5). Figure 4 supplement 2D should be brightened.

6). I would suggest that Figure 7B be transferred to the Figure supplement and that panels A and D of the Figure 7 supplement be transferred to the main Figure 7.

7). In general, the manuscript still requires a thorough revision by a native speaker as there are still many errors with many difficult to understand sentences.

claims.claim: The mammalian canonical SWI/SNF complex contains a core set of subunits consisting of BAF155 (SMARCC1), SMARCB1 (hSNF5 or INI1), and BAF170 (SMARCC2).
claims.source: In mammalian cells, the canonical SWI/SNF complex contains one of the two mutually exclusive ATPases, BRM (SMARCA2) or BRG1 (SMARCA4), in addition to a core set of subunits consisting of BAF155 (BRG1-associated factor or SMARCC1), SMARCB1 (hSNF5 or INI1), and BAF170 (SMARCC2), as well as four to eight accessory subunits (Khavari et al., 1993; Wang et al., 1996a; Wang et al., 1996b).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: The SWI/SNF complex mediates modifications on the nucleosome structure and regulates nucleosome positioning in an ATP-dependent manner.
claims.source: Importantly, the SWI/SNF complex mediates modifications on the nucleosome structure and regulates nucleosome positioning in an ATP-dependent manner, thereby modulating the accessibility of regulatory proteins.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about SWI/SNF function.

claims.claim: The SWI/SNF chromatin remodeling complex is critical for gene transcription, cell-cycle regulation, and cell differentiation.
claims.source: Therefore, this chromatin remodeling complex is critical for various biological processes, including gene transcription, cell-cycle regulation, and cell differentiation (Ho et al., 2009; Ho et al., 2009; Hodges et al., 2016; Kim and Roberts, 2014; Tolstorukov et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: IP4 and IP5 stimulate the activity of the SWI/SNF complex in yeast in vitro.
claims.source: A previous study in yeast demonstrated that IPs can regulate the nucleosome-sliding activity of chromatin remodeling complexes in vitro (Shen et al., 2003). Specifically, IP4 and IP5 stimulate the activity of the SWI/SNF complex, whereas inositol hexakisphosphate (IP6) inhibits the activity of the NURF, ISW2, and INO80 complexes.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from a previous study supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Inositol hexakisphosphate (IP6) inhibits the activity of the NURF, ISW2, and INO80 complexes in yeast in vitro.
claims.source: Specifically, IP4 and IP5 stimulate the activity of the SWI/SNF complex, whereas inositol hexakisphosphate (IP6) inhibits the activity of the NURF, ISW2, and INO80 complexes.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from a previous study supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Mutation in the yeast IPMK homolog Arg82 impairs IP4 and IP5 production.
claims.source: Another study in yeast illustrated that mutation in the yeast IPMK homolog Arg82 impairs IP4 and IP5 production and causes inefficient recruitment of the SWI/SNF complex and impaired chromatin remodeling at the promoter of the phosphate-responsive gene PHO5 (Steger et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from a previous study supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Mutation in the yeast IPMK homolog Arg82 causes inefficient recruitment of the SWI/SNF complex at the promoter of the phosphate-responsive gene PHO5.
claims.source: Another study in yeast illustrated that mutation in the yeast IPMK homolog Arg82 impairs IP4 and IP5 production and causes inefficient recruitment of the SWI/SNF complex and impaired chromatin remodeling at the promoter of the phosphate-responsive gene PHO5 (Steger et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from a previous study supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Mutation in the yeast IPMK homolog Arg82 causes impaired chromatin remodeling at the promoter of the phosphate-responsive gene PHO5.
claims.source: Another study in yeast illustrated that mutation in the yeast IPMK homolog Arg82 impairs IP4 and IP5 production and causes inefficient recruitment of the SWI/SNF complex and impaired chromatin remodeling at the promoter of the phosphate-responsive gene PHO5 (Steger et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from a previous study supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Inositol hexakisphosphate kinase 1 (IP6K1) directly interacts with histone demethylase JMJD2C in mammals.
claims.source: In mammals, inositol hexakisphosphate kinase 1 (IP6K1) directly interacts with histone demethylase JMJD2C. IP6K1 and its product 5-IP7 appear to mediate the expression of JMJDC2 target genes in mammalian cells by regulating the chromatin association of JMJDC2 and the levels of trimethyl-histone H3 lysine 9 (Burton et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from a previous study supported by a citation.

claims.claim: IP6K1 and its product 5-IP7 mediate the expression of JMJDC2 target genes in mammalian cells by regulating the chromatin association of JMJDC2 and the levels of trimethyl-histone H3 lysine 9.
claims.source: IP6K1 and its product 5-IP7 appear to mediate the expression of JMJDC2 target genes in mammalian cells by regulating the chromatin association of JMJDC2 and the levels of trimethyl-histone H3 lysine 9 (Burton et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a finding from a previous study supported by a citation.

claims.claim: SMARCB1 was identified as a potential IPMK-binding protein in yeast two-hybrid screening.
claims.source: The co-transformants of GAL4-DB fusion plasmid pGBKT7-IPMK (prey) and GAL4-AD fusion plasmid pACT2-SMARCB1 (bait) activated expression of the reporter gene, demonstrating cell growth on selective media, unlike the co-transformants of pGBKT-7 and pACT2-SMARCB1 (Figure 1A). Approximately 23–36 proteins were identified as potential interactors with IPMK (Supplementary file 1). Among these putative targets, only SMARCB1 was present in the results for both duplicates of the yeast two-hybrid screening (Supplementary file 1). These results indicate SMARCB1, a core subunit of the SWI/SNF chromatin remodeler, as a potential IPMK-binding protein.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from yeast two-hybrid screening experiments shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: SMARCB1 was the only protein present in both duplicates of the yeast two-hybrid screening for IPMK interactors.
claims.source: Among these putative targets, only SMARCB1 was present in the results for both duplicates of the yeast two-hybrid screening (Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a result from the yeast two-hybrid screening.

claims.claim: APEX2-mediated proximity labeling identified factors associated with the SWI/SNF complex, including SMARCB1, BRG1, SMARCC2, ARID1A, PBRM1, and SMARCC1, as IPMK interactors.
claims.source: Among these candidates, we detected factors associated with the SWI/SNF complex, including SMARCB1 (BAF47), BRG1 (SMARCA4), SMARCC2 (BAF170), ARID1A (BAF250A), PBRM1 (BAF180), and SMARCC1 (BAF155), as IPMK interactors (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from APEX2-mediated proximity labeling shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: SMARCB1 had the most significant interaction with IPMK among SWI/SNF complex subunits in APEX2-mediated proximity labeling.
claims.source: Furthermore, among these SWI/SNF complex subunits, SMARCB1 had the most significant interaction with IPMK or was positioned very proximal to IPMK (Figure 1C), consistent with the yeast two-hybrid screening results (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a result from APEX2-mediated proximity labeling shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: Core histones (histones H2B, H3.1, and H4) were detected as IPMK interactors in APEX2-mediated proximity labeling.
claims.source: We also detected core histones (histones H2B, H3.1, and H4) as IPMK interactors (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), supporting that IPMK interacts with the SWI/SNF complex, which binds to nucleosomes in vivo.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a result from APEX2-mediated proximity labeling shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: IPMK directly binds to SMARCB1 in vitro.
claims.source: To validate the physical interaction between IPMK and SMARCB1, we performed an in vitro binding assay using recombinant IPMK and SMARCB1 proteins. We detected a direct protein-protein interaction between IPMK and SMARCB1 (Figure 2A, see lane 2 and lane 4).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from in vitro binding assays shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: IPMK directly interacts with SMARCB1, BRG1, and BAF155 in vitro in Sf9 insect cells.
claims.source: We co-infected Sf9 insect cells with baculoviruses expressing FLAG-IPMK and individual subunits of the SWI/SNF complex, including SMARCB1, BRG1, BAF155 (SMARCC1), and BAF170 (SMARCC2). Next, we performed FLAG M2 agarose immunoprecipitation followed by immunoblotting. We detected direct interaction of IPMK with each of the SMARCB1, BRG1, and BAF155 proteins, but not with BAF170 (Figure 2B, see lane 7 and lane 8).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from binary protein-interaction assays shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: IPMK does not directly interact with BAF170 in vitro in Sf9 insect cells.
claims.source: We detected direct interaction of IPMK with each of the SMARCB1, BRG1, and BAF155 proteins, but not with BAF170 (Figure 2B, see lane 7 and lane 8).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from binary protein-interaction assays shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Endogenous IPMK and SMARCB1 directly associate in mouse embryonic stem cells.
claims.source: To investigate whether the interactions we observed also occur in vivo, we performed co-immunoprecipitation experiments with mammalian cells. We detected a direct association between endogenous IPMK and SMARCB1 in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs; Figure 2C and D) and in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 2C and D.

claims.claim: Endogenous IPMK and SMARCB1 directly associate in mouse embryonic fibroblasts.
claims.source: We detected a direct association between endogenous IPMK and SMARCB1 in mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs; Figure 2C and D) and in mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C.

claims.claim: SMARCB1, BRG1, and BAF155 co-immunoprecipitate with endogenous IPMK in mESC extracts.
claims.source: Consistent with our in vitro binding assays (Figure 2A and B), SMARCB1, BRG1, and BAF155 co-immunoprecipitated with endogenous IPMK (Figure 2C) and overexpressed FLAG-IPMK (Figure 2E) in mESC extracts.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: SMARCB1, BRG1, and BAF155 co-immunoprecipitate with overexpressed FLAG-IPMK in mESC extracts.
claims.source: Consistent with our in vitro binding assays (Figure 2A and B), SMARCB1, BRG1, and BAF155 co-immunoprecipitated with endogenous IPMK (Figure 2C) and overexpressed FLAG-IPMK (Figure 2E) in mESC extracts.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: SMARCB1, BRG1, and BAF170 were detected in IPMK immunoprecipitates from MEF extracts.
claims.source: Intriguingly, we detected SMARCB1, BRG1, and BAF170 in the IPMK immunoprecipitates from MEF extracts (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, B.

claims.claim: IPMK knockdown does not affect the protein levels of SWI/SNF complex subunits in mESCs or MEFs.
claims.source: We observed that IpmkKD did not affect the protein levels of the SWI/SNF complex subunits and Smarcb1KD did not affect the IPMK protein levels in mESCs or MEFs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from knockdown experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: SMARCB1 knockdown does not affect IPMK protein levels in mESCs or MEFs.
claims.source: We observed that IpmkKD did not affect the protein levels of the SWI/SNF complex subunits and Smarcb1KD did not affect the IPMK protein levels in mESCs or MEFs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from knockdown experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: IPMK knockdown significantly reduces SMARCB1 signals in IPMK immunoprecipitates from mESCs.
claims.source: Importantly, a significant reduction in SMARCB1 signals was observed in the IPMK immunoprecipitate from IpmkKD mESCs compared to control (EgfpKD) mESCs (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from knockdown and immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: SMARCB1 knockdown significantly reduces SMARCB1 and BRG1 signals in IPMK immunoprecipitates from MEFs.
claims.source: We also found that the SMARCB1 and BRG1 signals in IPMK immunoprecipitate from SmarcbKD MEFs were significantly decreased compared to signals in the control (EgfpKD) MEFs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from knockdown and immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claims.claim: IPMK-null MEFs show a significant reduction in IPMK signals in SMARCB1 immunoprecipitates.
claims.source: Furthermore, in SMARCB1 immunoprecipitate, we detected a significant reduction in IPMK signals in IPMK-null MEFs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from immunoprecipitation experiments in IPMK-null MEFs shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: IPMK physically interacts with SMARCB1 in HEK293T cells.
claims.source: To confirm this, we performed a co-immunoprecipitation assay by co-expressing IPMK and SMARCB1 in HEK293T cells. Consistent with the above results, we observed a physical interaction between IPMK and SMARCB1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claims.claim: Core subunits of the SWI/SNF (BAF)/PBAF complexes (SMARCB1, BAF155, BAF170, PBRM1, BAF250A, and BRM) were pulled down with GST-IPMK in HEK293T cells.
claims.source: Next, we performed GST pull-down assays by overexpressing GST-IPMK or GST alone (negative control) in HEK293T cells. Notably, the core subunits of the SWI/SNF (BAF)/PBAF complexes, namely SMARCB1, BAF155, BAF170, PBRM1, BAF250A, and BRM, were pulled down alongside GST-IPMK (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G), which was not seen in the negative control.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from GST pull-down assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G.

claims.claim: Core subunits of the SWI/SNF complex (SMARCB1, BRG1, BAF155, and BAF170) were detected in GST-IPMK pull-downs with purified SWI/SNF complexes.
claims.source: Lastly, we purified endogenous SWI/SNF (BAF) complexes from cells expressing FLAG-DPF2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H). We co-incubated the purified SWI/SNF complexes with purified GST-IPMK or GST alone and performed GST pull-down assays. As expected, we detected the core subunits of the SWI/SNF complex (SMARCB1, BRG1, BAF155, and BAF170) in GST-IPMK pull-downs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from GST pull-down assays with purified complexes shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1I.

claims.claim: The Rpt1 and Rpt2 domains of SMARCB1 participate in the protein-protein interactions between SMARCB1 and IPMK.
claims.source: Interestingly, the prey vectors expressing amino acids 99–245, 99–319, and full-length SMARCB1 resulted in positive signals in the two-hybrid system (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), indicating that the Rpt1 and Rpt2 domains of SMARCB1 participate in the protein-protein interactions between SMARCB1 and IPMK.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from yeast two-hybrid assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The Rpt1 domain of SMARCB1 is essential for the IPMK interaction.
claims.source: We confirmed that the Rpt1 domain of SMARCB1 is essential for the IPMK interaction by immunoprecipitating the overexpressed deletion constructs (Figure 3B, compare lane 3 with lanes 2, 4, and 5).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from immunoprecipitation experiments with deletion constructs shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Both the Rpt1 and Rpt2 domains of SMARCB1 can bind to IPMK.
claims.source: By independently overexpressing each SMARCB1 domain, we found that both the Rpt1 and Rpt2 domains of SMARCB1 could bind to IPMK (Figure 3D and E, see lanes 3, 4, and 6).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 3D and E.

claims.claim: In Rpt1, two β-sheets and two α-helices are required for IPMK binding.
claims.source: In Rpt1, two β-sheets and two α-helices are required for IPMK binding (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, compare lane 4 with lanes 2 and 3).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: In Rpt2, only two β-sheets and no α-helices were bound to IPMK.
claims.source: In Rpt2, only two β-sheets and no α-helices were bound to IPMK (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, compare lane 2 with lane 3).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: SMARCB1 lacking Rpt1 and Rpt2 is not able to bind IPMK.
claims.source: This was further confirmed by the SMARCB1 lacking Rpt1 and Rpt2 not being able to bind IPMK (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E, compare lane 2 with lane 3, and F).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and F.

claims.claim: The sheets/helices of Rpt1 and sheets of Rpt2 are the major IPMK-interacting sites in SMARCB1.
claims.source: Thus, we concluded that the sheets/helices of Rpt1 and sheets of Rpt2 are the major IPMK-interacting sites in SMARCB1.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple domain mapping experiments.

claims.claim: IPMK-SMARCB1 binding is primarily mediated by three IPMK regions, including exon 3, exon 4, and exon 6.
claims.source: IPMK-SMARCB1 binding was primarily mediated by three IPMK regions, including exon 3, exon 4, and exon 6 (Figure 3F, lanes 4, 5, 7, and 8 show positive signals, and Figure 3G), which comprise the inositol binding site and the kinase domain.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from immunoprecipitation experiments with IPMK deletion constructs shown in Figure 3F and G.

claims.claim: IPMK is evenly distributed in cytoplasm, nucleoplasm, and chromatin fractions in mESCs and MEFs.
claims.source: IPMK was evenly distributed in all the three subcellular fractions (cytoplasm, nucleoplasm, and chromatin), whereas SMARCB1 and BRG1 were primarily found in the chromatin fraction for both mESCs and MEFs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-D).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from chromatin fractionation assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-D.

claims.claim: SMARCB1 and BRG1 are primarily found in the chromatin fraction in mESCs and MEFs.
claims.source: IPMK was evenly distributed in all the three subcellular fractions (cytoplasm, nucleoplasm, and chromatin), whereas SMARCB1 and BRG1 were primarily found in the chromatin fraction for both mESCs and MEFs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-D).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from chromatin fractionation assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-D.

claims.claim: IPMK knockdown does not affect the distribution of SMARCB1 in mESCs.
claims.source: We observed that the distribution of SMARCB1 was unaffected by IpmkKD (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), and the distribution of IPMK was unaffected by Smarcb1KD (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from chromatin fractionation assays after knockdown shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: SMARCB1 knockdown does not affect the distribution of IPMK in mESCs.
claims.source: We observed that the distribution of SMARCB1 was unaffected by IpmkKD (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), and the distribution of IPMK was unaffected by Smarcb1KD (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from chromatin fractionation assays after knockdown shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: IPMK co-localizes with BRG1 on the genome in mESCs.
claims.source: To investigate the localization of BRG1 and IPMK within the chromatin, we performed cleavage under targets and release using nuclease (CUT&RUN) assays (Skene and Henikoff, 2017) in mESCs. In accordance with our results showing the physical association of IPMK and the SWI/SNF complex, we found that IPMK co-localizes with BRG1 on the genome (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from CUT&RUN assays shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: BRG1 is significantly enriched at promoters in the mouse genome.
claims.source: Given that BRG1, a catalytic subunit of the SWI/SNF complex, is known to localize at the promoter-TSS (de Dieuleveult et al., 2016), we confirmed that BRG1 is significantly enriched at promoters in the mouse genome (Figure 4E and F).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from peak annotation analysis shown in Figure 4E and F, consistent with prior knowledge.

claims.claim: IPMK is significantly enriched at promoters in the mouse genome.
claims.source: Notably, IPMK was also significantly enriched at promoters (Figure 4E and F).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from peak annotation analysis shown in Figure 4E and F.

claims.claim: Highly enriched BRG1 CUT&RUN peaks mostly localize at enhancers in mESCs.
claims.source: Consistent with previous findings, highly enriched BRG1 chromatin immunoprecipitation sequencing (ChIP-seq) peaks from the previous study (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E) and highly enriched BRG1 CUT&RUN peaks from our study (Figure 4B and D, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F) mostly localized at enhancers (upper part of the heatmap).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from CUT&RUN analysis shown in Figure 4B, D, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claims.claim: Highly enriched IPMK localizes at enhancers in mESCs.
claims.source: Notably, we found that highly enriched IPMK also localized at enhancers (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from CUT&RUN analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: IPMK knockdown significantly reduces genome-wide BRG1 intensity at BRG1 CUT&RUN peaks with low BRG1 enrichment in mESCs.
claims.source: Interestingly, we detected a significant reduction in genome-wide BRG1 intensity upon IpmkKD at BRG1 CUT&RUN peaks, with low BRG1 enrichment in EgfpKD mESCs (bottom half of the heatmaps, termed as Low; Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from CUT&RUN assays after IPMK knockdown shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: shRNA-mediated IPMK silencing significantly reduces genome-wide BRG1 intensity at BRG1 CUT&RUN peaks with low BRG1 enrichment in mESCs.
claims.source: Consistent with the decreased BRG1 intensity shown in siRNA-mediated Ipmk silencing (Figure 4B), we detected a significant reduction in genome-wide BRG1 intensity upon shRNA-mediated Ipmk silencing at BRG1 CUT&RUN peaks with low BRG1 enrichment in shNT mESCs (bottom half of the heatmaps, termed as Low; Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from CUT&RUN assays after shRNA-mediated IPMK silencing shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: The reduction in BRG1 intensity at Low BRG1 peaks upon IPMK depletion is not derived from changes in the expression of BRG1 or other subunits of the SWI/SNF complex.
claims.source: The observed reduction in BRG1 intensity at Low BRG1 peaks was not derived from any changes in the expression of BRG1 or other subunits of the SWI/SNF complex (Figure 2—figure supplement 1DFigure 4—figure supplement 1B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and C), excluding the possibility that IPMK depletion results in reduced expression of BRG1 or another SWI/SNF complex subunit that leads to reduced BRG1 occupancy.
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from immunoblotting data shown in multiple figures.

claims.claim: IPMK depletion does not affect the global distribution of BRG1 CUT&RUN peaks.
claims.source: In addition, the genomic distribution of BRG1 CUT&RUN peaks was unaffected by IpmkKD (Figure 4E and F), suggesting that IPMK depletion does not affect the global distribution (changes in peak positions) of BRG1, but impacts the global occupancy of BRG1, especially at the low-enriched BRG1 peaks (Low), which do not correlate with enhancers (Figure 4B and D).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from peak annotation analysis shown in Figure 4E and F.

claims.claim: IPMK depletion impacts the global occupancy of BRG1, especially at low-enriched BRG1 peaks.
claims.source: In addition, the genomic distribution of BRG1 CUT&RUN peaks was unaffected by IpmkKD (Figure 4E and F), suggesting that IPMK depletion does not affect the global distribution (changes in peak positions) of BRG1, but impacts the global occupancy of BRG1, especially at the low-enriched BRG1 peaks (Low), which do not correlate with enhancers (Figure 4B and D).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from CUT&RUN data shown in Figure 4B, D, E, and F.

claims.claim: Wild-type IPMK transfection significantly increases BRG1 intensity compared to IPMK knockdown mESCs.
claims.source: Although +WT transfection did not fully restore the BRG1 intensity, we observed a significantly increased BRG1 intensity in IpmkKD +WT compared to IpmkKD mESCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 2G and H).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from rescue experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2G and H.

claims.claim: Catalytically dead IPMK transfection significantly increases BRG1 intensity compared to IPMK knockdown mESCs.
claims.source: Interestingly, +SA transfection also exhibited significantly increased BRG1 intensity compared to IpmkKD mESCs and did not show a large difference in BRG1 intensity compared to IpmkKD +WT mESCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 2G and H).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from rescue experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2G and H.

claims.claim: The enzymatic activity of IPMK is not required for the regulation of BRG1 occupancy in mESCs.
claims.source: These results indicate that the enzymatic activity of IPMK is not required for the regulation of BRG1 occupancy in mESCs.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from rescue experiments with catalytically dead IPMK.

claims.claim: BRG1 regulates chromatin accessibility at nucleosome free regions (NFRs) of TSS in mESCs.
claims.source: BRG1 was previously shown to regulate chromatin accessibility at nucleosome free regions (NFRs) of TSS in mESCs (de Dieuleveult et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is stated as prior knowledge supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Global BRG1 occupancy is reduced upon IPMK knockdown at BRG1 peaks with low BRG1 intensity.
claims.source: As expected, we observed that the global BRG1 occupancy was reduced upon IpmkKD at BRG1 peaks with low BRG1 intensity (Low; Figure 4G), consistent with our previous observations (Figure 4B).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from CUT&RUN analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: Both BRG1 occupancy and BRG1-mediated chromatin accessibility are significantly reduced upon IPMK knockdown at Low BRG1 peaks in a genome-wide manner.
claims.source: Importantly, at Low BRG1 peaks, both BRG1 occupancy and BRG1-mediated chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq signals closest to the BRG1 CUT&RUN peaks) were significantly reduced upon IpmkKD in a genome-wide manner (Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 2I).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from CUT&RUN and ATAC-seq analysis shown in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 2I.

claims.claim: IPMK depletion greatly reduces BRG1 and ATAC-seq intensity, especially at Low BRG1 peaks.
claims.source: Notably, when comparing the highly enriched (High) and lowly enriched (Low) BRG1 peaks, IPMK depletion greatly reduced the BRG1 and ATAC-seq intensity, especially at Low BRG1 peaks (Figure 4H).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from CUT&RUN and ATAC-seq analysis shown in Figure 4H.

claims.claim: Reduced BRG1 and BRG1-associated chromatin accessibility upon IPMK knockdown are detected at Low BRG1 peaks residing at promoter-TSS regions.
claims.source: Reduced BRG1 and BRG1-associated chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) upon IpmkKD were also detected Low BRG1 peaks residing at promoter-TSS regions (Figure 4I), consistent with the previous study in which BRG1 primarily maintained chromatin accessibility at promoter-TSS regions (de Dieuleveult et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from CUT&RUN and ATAC-seq analysis shown in Figure 4I, consistent with prior knowledge.

claims.claim: IPMK regulates the global BRG1 occupancy and corresponding BRG1-mediated chromatin accessibility in mESCs.
claims.source: Taken together, these results indicate that IPMK regulates the global BRG1 occupancy and corresponding BRG1-mediated chromatin accessibility in mESCs.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple CUT&RUN and ATAC-seq experiments.

claims.claim: BRG1 is abundant near TSSs in mESCs.
claims.source: We confirmed that BRG1 is abundant near TSSs and observed two major BRG1 peaks, which were divided by the TSS and coincided with the –1 and +1 nucleosomes (Figure 5A, left).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from analysis of BRG1 CUT&RUN data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: Two major BRG1 peaks are divided by the TSS and coincide with the –1 and +1 nucleosomes in mESCs.
claims.source: We confirmed that BRG1 is abundant near TSSs and observed two major BRG1 peaks, which were divided by the TSS and coincided with the –1 and +1 nucleosomes (Figure 5A, left).

results.result: IPMK physically interacts with SWI/SNF complex subunits. Yeast two-hybrid screening identified SMARCB1 as the only protein present in both duplicates (C37, C38). APEX2-mediated proximity labeling identified multiple SWI/SNF subunits including SMARCB1, BRG1, SMARCC2, ARID1A, PBRM1, and SMARCC1 as IPMK interactors, with SMARCB1 showing the most significant interaction (C39, C40). Core histones were also detected as IPMK interactors (C41).
results.evaluation: Two independent unbiased screening methods (yeast two-hybrid and APEX2 proximity labeling) converge on identifying SMARCB1 and other SWI/SNF subunits as IPMK interactors (C37-C41). The consistency between methods and detection of histones (which bind to SWI/SNF-associated nucleosomes) provides strong support. However, proximity labeling detects proteins in close spatial proximity, not necessarily direct binding.

results.result: IPMK directly binds to SMARCB1, BRG1, and BAF155 in vitro and in vivo. In vitro binding assays demonstrated direct IPMK-SMARCB1 interaction (C42). Binary protein-interaction assays in Sf9 cells showed IPMK directly interacts with SMARCB1, BRG1, and BAF155, but not BAF170 (C43, C44). Co-immunoprecipitation experiments confirmed endogenous IPMK-SMARCB1 association in mESCs and MEFs (C45-C49). GST pull-down assays with purified complexes further validated these interactions (C55-C57).
results.evaluation: Multiple orthogonal approaches (in vitro binding, binary interaction assays, co-IP in multiple cell types, GST pull-downs with purified complexes) consistently demonstrate direct physical interactions between IPMK and specific SWI/SNF subunits (C42-C49, C55-C57). The specificity is demonstrated by lack of interaction with BAF170 in some assays. The convergence of evidence from different experimental systems strongly supports direct binding.

results.result: IPMK and SMARCB1 knockdowns do not affect each other's protein levels but reduce co-immunoprecipitation signals. IPMK knockdown does not affect SWI/SNF subunit protein levels, and SMARCB1 knockdown does not affect IPMK levels (C50, C51). However, IPMK knockdown significantly reduces SMARCB1 signals in IPMK immunoprecipitates (C52), SMARCB1 knockdown reduces SMARCB1 and BRG1 signals in IPMK immunoprecipitates (C53), and IPMK-null MEFs show reduced IPMK signals in SMARCB1 immunoprecipitates (C54).
results.evaluation: The knockdown experiments demonstrate that the interaction is not mediated by changes in protein expression levels (C50, C51), and the reduced co-IP signals upon knockdown confirm specificity of the interaction (C52-C54). This provides important controls showing the interaction is direct rather than mediated by expression changes.

results.result: The Rpt1 and Rpt2 domains of SMARCB1 and exons 3, 4, and 6 of IPMK mediate their interaction. Yeast two-hybrid and immunoprecipitation with deletion constructs mapped the interaction to Rpt1 and Rpt2 domains of SMARCB1 (C58-C64), with specific structural requirements (β-sheets and α-helices in Rpt1, β-sheets in Rpt2). The IPMK-SMARCB1 binding is mediated by IPMK exons 3, 4, and 6, comprising the inositol binding site and kinase domain (C65).
results.evaluation: Systematic domain mapping using yeast two-hybrid and deletion constructs in mammalian cells consistently identifies specific domains required for interaction (C58-C65). The structural detail (specific β-sheets and α-helices) and reciprocal mapping of both proteins provides strong support. However, the functional significance of these specific domains is not tested.

results.result: IPMK co-localizes with BRG1 on chromatin at promoters and enhancers. Chromatin fractionation showed IPMK is distributed across cytoplasm, nucleoplasm, and chromatin, while SMARCB1 and BRG1 are primarily in chromatin (C66, C67). Knockdowns do not affect subcellular distribution (C68, C69). CUT&RUN assays demonstrated IPMK co-localizes with BRG1 genome-wide (C70), with both significantly enriched at promoters (C71, C72). Highly enriched BRG1 and IPMK localize at enhancers (C73, C74).
results.evaluation: CUT&RUN data directly demonstrates genome-wide co-localization of IPMK and BRG1 (C70-C74), consistent with physical interaction data. The chromatin fractionation provides supporting evidence that both proteins are present on chromatin (C66-C69). Peak annotation analysis confirms enrichment at functionally relevant genomic regions (promoters and enhancers).

results.result: IPMK depletion reduces BRG1 occupancy at low-enriched BRG1 peaks in a kinase-independent manner. Both siRNA and shRNA-mediated IPMK depletion significantly reduced BRG1 intensity at low BRG1 peaks (C75, C76). This reduction is not due to changes in BRG1 or SWI/SNF subunit expression (C77) or changes in peak distribution (C78), but affects global BRG1 occupancy at low-enriched peaks (C79). Rescue experiments with wild-type and catalytically dead IPMK both increased BRG1 intensity, indicating enzymatic activity is not required (C80-C82).
results.evaluation: Multiple lines of evidence support that IPMK regulates BRG1 occupancy: consistent effects with different knockdown methods (C75, C76), appropriate controls excluding indirect effects (C77, C78), and rescue experiments demonstrating kinase-independent function (C80-C82). The specificity for low BRG1 peaks is well-documented (C79). The rescue with catalytically dead IPMK is particularly important for mechanism.

results.result: IPMK regulates BRG1-mediated chromatin accessibility genome-wide. IPMK knockdown reduced BRG1 occupancy at low BRG1 peaks (C84), and both BRG1 occupancy and chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq) were significantly reduced at these peaks genome-wide (C85, C86). This effect was detected at low BRG1 peaks at promoter-TSS regions (C87), leading to the conclusion that IPMK regulates global BRG1 occupancy and chromatin accessibility (C88).
results.evaluation: The integration of CUT&RUN and ATAC-seq data demonstrates that IPMK depletion affects both BRG1 localization and chromatin accessibility (C84-C87). The genome-wide analysis and focus on promoter-TSS regions provides comprehensive evidence. The correlation between reduced BRG1 and reduced chromatin accessibility supports a functional consequence of the interaction.

results.result: BRG1 localizes at -1 and +1 nucleosomes flanking TSSs in mESCs. Analysis of BRG1 CUT&RUN, MNase-seq, and ATAC-seq showed BRG1 is abundant near TSSs with two major peaks at -1 and +1 nucleosomes (C89, C90). Nucleosome-depleted regions (NFRs) are present at TSSs (C91). BRG1 intensity and chromatin accessibility vary by promoter type (high in H3K4me3-Only, moderate in bivalent, low in H3K4me3-Low) (C92). IPMK knockdown reduces BRG1 occupancy at both H3K4me3-Only and bivalent promoters (C93).
results.evaluation: The integration of multiple genomic datasets (CUT&RUN, MNase-seq, ATAC-seq) provides strong evidence for BRG1 localization patterns (C89-C92). The promoter classification method is validated by consistency with prior studies. The effect of IPMK knockdown on different promoter types is well-documented (C93).

results.result: IPMK depletion preferentially affects chromatin accessibility at bivalent promoters. ATAC-seq signals were significantly reduced upon IPMK knockdown at both promoter types (C96), with similar effects to BRG1 knockdown (C97). However, bivalent promoters showed greater reduction than H3K4me3-Only promoters (C98, C99). H3K4me3-Only promoters retain more BRG1 after IPMK knockdown (C100). The authors conclude IPMK plays a pivotal role in maintaining chromatin accessibility at bivalent promoters by safeguarding BRG1 occupancy at -1 nucleosomes (C104-C106).
results.evaluation: The differential effect on bivalent vs. H3K4me3-Only promoters is well-documented with ATAC-seq data (C96-C99). The mechanistic explanation involving remaining BRG1 levels and compensatory chromatin remodelers is supported by the data (C100). However, the conclusion about -1 nucleosome specificity (C104-C106) is somewhat inferential, relying on integration with prior studies rather than direct demonstration in this work.

results.result: IPMK depletion reduces gene expression, particularly at bivalent promoters. mRNA levels of genes with H3K4me3-Only or bivalent promoters were down-regulated upon IPMK knockdown (C107), with greater down-regulation at bivalent promoters (C108). RT-qPCR confirmed down-regulation of genes with decreased BRG1 occupancy and reduced ATAC-seq signals (C109). BRG1 occupancy and chromatin accessibility were both reduced near TSSs of down-regulated genes (C111). The authors conclude IPMK maintains gene expression by safeguarding BRG1 occupancy and chromatin accessibility at promoter-TSSs (C112).
results.evaluation: The integration of mRNA-seq, CUT&RUN, and ATAC-seq data demonstrates correlation between IPMK depletion, reduced BRG1 occupancy, reduced chromatin accessibility, and reduced gene expression (C107-C112). However, the causal relationship is inferential - the data show correlation but do not definitively prove that reduced BRG1 occupancy causes reduced expression. Additional experiments (e.g., rescue of specific genes) would strengthen causality.

results.result: IPMK regulates endodermal gene expression during mESC differentiation. During EB formation, pluripotency markers decreased similarly in control and IPMK-depleted cells (C113), but endodermal markers (Foxa1, Foxa2, Gata6, Sox17) showed significantly decreased levels upon IPMK depletion from day 0 onwards (C114, C115). Ectodermal and mesodermal markers showed minimal or no changes (C116-C118). IPMK depletion had the most severe impact on endodermal markers (C119). All reduced endodermal markers have bivalent promoters in mESCs (C120), and most showed decreased BRG1 occupancy upon IPMK depletion (C121, C122). BRG1 depletion similarly decreased endodermal marker expression (C123), suggesting IPMK regulates these genes through BRG1 (C124).
results.evaluation: The EB differentiation experiments demonstrate specific effects on endodermal lineage markers (C113-C119). The connection to bivalent promoters and reduced BRG1 occupancy provides a mechanistic link to earlier findings (C120-C122). The parallel effects of BRG1 depletion support the proposed mechanism (C123). However, the conclusion that IPMK regulates endodermal development (C124) is somewhat overstated - the data show effects on marker gene expression but do not demonstrate functional consequences for lineage commitment or differentiation efficiency.

results.result: IPMK preferentially regulates BRG1 occupancy at regions with low BRG1 levels. The authors conclude that IPMK depletion has greater impact at low BRG1 peaks compared to high BRG1 peaks (C125), with greater effects on bivalent promoters (low BRG1) than H3K4me3-Only promoters (high BRG1) (C126). They propose IPMK primarily regulates BRG1 occupancy and downstream effects at regions with originally low BRG1 levels (C127).
results.evaluation: This is a synthesis of multiple results throughout the paper (C125-C127). The pattern is consistently observed across different analyses (CUT&RUN, ATAC-seq, mRNA-seq) and promoter classifications. However, the mechanistic explanation for this context-dependency is speculative and not directly tested.

results.result: Proposed model: IPMK physically binds SWI/SNF subunits to maintain BRG1 occupancy and chromatin accessibility. The authors propose a model where IPMK physically binds SMARCB1, BRG1, and BAF155, maintaining appropriate BRG1 occupancy and chromatin accessibility at promoter-TSSs, thereby regulating gene expression (C128). When IPMK is depleted, BRG1 localization is perturbed and chromatin accessibility decreased (C129).
results.evaluation: This model integrates the major findings of the paper: physical interaction (C6, C42-C49), co-localization (C70-C74), regulation of BRG1 occupancy (C75-C88), effects on chromatin accessibility (C84-C106), and gene expression (C107-C124). The model is well-supported by the data, though the precise mechanism by which IPMK regulates BRG1 localization remains unclear.

results.result: Background on IPMK function. IPMK is a key enzyme in IP metabolism (C1, C14) and a pleiotropic signaling factor (C2) that acts as a PI3-kinase producing PIP3 (C15) and non-catalytically controls mTOR, AMPK, and TRAF6 (C16). Nuclear IPMK regulates gene expression (C17), originally identified in yeast as Arg82 (C18), which interacts with MCM1 (C19, C20). In mammals, IPMK-SRF binding is critical for gene expression (C21), and IPMK interacts with p53, SF1, and CBP/p300 (C22).
results.evaluation: These are established facts from prior literature, appropriately cited (C1, C2, C14-C22). They provide necessary background context but are not novel findings of this study.

results.result: Background on SWI/SNF and IP-chromatin remodeling connections. SWI/SNF plays a critical role in gene expression by regulating chromatin accessibility (C3, C4). Chromatin remodeling is essential for transcription (C23), and SWI/SNF is a large family of ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling complexes (C24, C25) with specific subunit composition (C26, C27) that regulates nucleosome positioning (C28) and is critical for transcription, cell cycle, and differentiation (C29). Prior yeast studies showed IP4/IP5 stimulate SWI/SNF while IP6 inhibits other remodelers (C30, C31), and Arg82 mutation impairs SWI/SNF recruitment (C32-C34). In mammals, IP6K1 interacts with JMJD2C to regulate gene expression (C35, C36).
results.evaluation: These are established facts from prior literature, appropriately cited (C3, C4, C23-C36). They provide necessary background on SWI/SNF function and prior connections between IPs and chromatin remodeling, motivating the current study.

results.result: Knowledge gap: The direct link between IPMK and chromatin remodelers remains unclear (C5).
results.evaluation: This accurately describes the knowledge gap that motivates the study (C5). The current work addresses this gap by demonstrating direct physical interactions.

results.result: Background on BRG1 function at promoters. BRG1 regulates chromatin accessibility at NFRs of TSSs (C83). BRG1 at -1 nucleosome in wide NFRs positively regulates accessibility, while BRG1 at +1 nucleosome in narrow NFRs tends to inhibit accessibility (C94, C95). Most chromatin remodelers show higher enrichment at H3K4me3-Only vs. bivalent promoters (C101). BRG1 depletion reduces ATAC-seq signals more at bivalent than H3K4me3-Only promoters (C103).
results.evaluation: These are established facts from prior literature (primarily de Dieuleveult et al., 2016), appropriately cited (C83, C94, C95, C101, C103). They provide necessary context for interpreting the current findings about differential effects at different promoter types.

results.result: Validation of prior findings: Various chromatin remodelers show higher occupancy at H3K4me3-Only vs. bivalent promoters. The authors analyzed publicly released data and confirmed that CHD1, CHD2, CHD4, CHD6, CHD8, CHD9, and EP400 show higher occupancy at H3K4me3-Only promoters compared to bivalent promoters (C102).
results.evaluation: This is a validation of prior findings using publicly available data (C102). It confirms the expected pattern and supports the interpretation that compensatory chromatin remodelers may explain differential effects at different promoter types.
